sec.title: Objectives
sec.p: Coffee is one of the most widely consumed beverages worldwide and a major cause of extrinsic staining in resin-based dental materials. This study evaluated the effects of different coffee types, along with their chlorogenic acid (CGA) and total phenolic content (TPC) levels, on the color stability, surface roughness, and microhardness of resin composites.

sec.title: Materials and methods
sec.p: The TPC and CGA levels of Turkish, filter, and instant coffee were quantified spectrophotometrically. A total of 120 disc-shaped specimens (8 × 2 mm) were fabricated from three resin composites: G-ænial A’Chord (GA, nanohybrid), Estelite Sigma Quick (ESQ, suprananohybrid), and Filtek Universal (FU, nanofilled). Baseline color, roughness, and microhardness values were recorded. Specimens were immersed in coffee solutions or distilled water for 7 and 30 days, after which measurements were repeated. Data were analyzed using IBM SPSS v25; normality was tested with the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, and homogeneity of variance with Levene’s test. A mixed-design three-way ANOVA with Tukey post hoc tests was used (α = 0.05).

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Color, surface roughness, and microhardness were significantly influenced by time, solution, and material. Discoloration was mainly solution-dependent, with instant coffee causing the greatest color change and GA showing better color stability than FU and ESQ. Surface roughness increased in all groups and microhardness decreased, most notably in filter and instant coffee; overall, FU showed the highest hardness and GA the lowest, while instant coffee had the highest phenolic/chlorogenic acid content.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: All coffee types produced clinically unacceptable discoloration (ΔE00 > 1.8), most pronounced with instant coffee, whereas GA showed superior color stability to FU and ESQ. Surface roughness increased but remained below the 0.2 μm plaque-retentive threshold, and microhardness losses were greatest in filter and instant coffee and smallest in Turkish coffee. These findings indicate that coffee composition and composite resin matrix/filler characteristics jointly influence staining and degradation.

sec.title: Clinical significance
sec.p: Considering phenolic content (TPC, CGA) and particulate load, coffee type and composition should guide material selection in heavy coffee drinkers, with more hydrophobic composites potentially improving long-term color stability. Different coffee types/brewing methods can variably effect staining, underscoring the need to counsel patients on diet-related discoloration.
Keywords: Chlorogenic acid, Discoloration, Microhardness, Surface roughness, Total phenolic content

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Resin composite materials are widely used in modern dentistry to meet both esthetic and functional requirements. They are particularly preferred in anterior regions due to their ability to mimic natural tooth structure in terms of color, gloss, and surface smoothness. However, their long-term clinical success depends not only on their initial physical and optical properties but also on the preservation of these characteristics over time [1].

Color stability is critical for maintaining the esthetic performance of restorations. It can be negatively influenced by dietary pigments, acidic beverages, tobacco use, and inadequate oral hygiene [2]. Coffee, owing to its content of chlorogenic acid (CGA), total phenolic compounds (TPC), melanoidins, and trigonelline, has been identified as a major factor contributing to extrinsic discoloration of both natural teeth and resin-based materials [2, 3].

Surface roughness also plays a key role in the esthetic and biological performance of restorations. Rough surfaces facilitate plaque accumulation, increase the risk of secondary caries, and promote extrinsic staining [3]. These properties are influenced by intrinsic factors such as matrix composition, filler size, and filler loading, as well as extrinsic factors including exposure to acidic or pigmented agents. Nanohybrid composites, with their multi-sized filler technology, are designed to provide a more homogeneous matrix [4]. Nevertheless, smaller filler size does not always correlate with lower roughness or reduced discoloration, as the monomer composition may also be a determining factor [4, 5].

The pigmenting and acidic properties of coffee can cause both physical and chemical alterations in composites, while its low pH may further promote the growth of acidophilic bacteria, indirectly increasing staining [2]. High CGA concentrations may enhance this effect by further lowering the pH (1); however, there is still no clear consensus in the literature regarding the precise role of CGA (2).

Preparation methods also influence the chemical composition of coffee. Filter coffee, prepared by hot brewing, generally contains higher levels of soluble pigments, melanoidins, and CGA [1]. Turkish coffee, obtained by boiling finely ground beans, has a high particle density that may increase surface contact and staining potential [6]. Instant coffee, produced by industrial drying methods, varies in its soluble composition depending on the manufacturing process, with some products reported to contain higher CGA levels than other coffee types [2].

Despite its clinical relevance, there is limited evidence comparing the effects of different coffee types on resin composites [2, 7]. Given the variations in preparation methods and chemical composition, a direct comparison of their impact on restorative materials is warranted.

Therefore, this study aimed to evaluate the effects of three coffee types (Turkish, filter, and instant coffee) and their CGA and TPC levels on resin composites. Two null hypotheses were tested: (1) different coffee types would not produce significant differences in discoloration, microhardness, or surface roughness; and (2) CGA and TPC levels would not differ significantly among the coffee types. Understanding these effects may provide clinicians with valuable insights for material selection and for counseling patients regarding the potential impact of coffee consumption on restoration longevity.

sec.title: Sample size calculation
sec.p: The sample size for this study was calculated using G*Power v3.1.9.2 for a mixed-design three-way ANOVA. The analysis was based on a medium effect size (f = 0.25), a significance level of α = 0.05, a desired statistical power of 1 − β = 0.80, 12 groups (3 materials × 4 solutions), and three repeated measurements (baseline, day 7, and day 30) [8], . The correlation among repeated measures was set at 0.50, and the nonsphericity correction (ε) was set to 1.00. The analysis indicated that a minimum total sample size of 72 specimens would be required. The actual sample size used in the study exceeded this requirement, and the achieved power of the model was 0.84, indicating that the statistical power of the study was adequate.

sec.title: Preparation of resin composite specimens
sec.p: In this study, three different resin composite materials were used: G-ænial A’Chord (GA; nanohybrid), Estelite Sigma Quick (ESQ; suprananohybrid), and Filtek Universal (FU; nanofilled; Table 1). A total of 120 disc-shaped specimens (8 mm in diameter and 2 mm in height) were prepared, with 40 specimens from each material. The resin composites were placed into Teflon molds using a metal spatula, covered with a Mylar strip and a 1 mm thick glass slide, and then polymerized for 20 s with a light-emitting diode (LED) curing unit (DTE LUX E, Borkstrasse, Münster, Germany) at a light intensity of 1000 mW/cm², with the glass slide in contact with the material.

sec.p: For surface finishing, medium and superfine aluminum oxide discs (Optidisc, Kerr, USA) were used, with each disc discarded after a single use. The discs were applied for 20 s using a low-speed handpiece (NSK Ti-Max, Japan) operating at 5000 rpm, with circular motions and light pressure. All finishing and polishing procedures were performed in random order by a single operator who was blinded to the material type [9, 10]. After light-curing, the final thickness of all specimens after finishing and polishing was measured using a digital micrometer (± 0.01 mm; Mitutoyo, Japan) and the specimens were then stored in distilled water at 37 °C for 24 h to allow for post-polymerization.

sec.title: Preparation of coffee solutions and immersion protocol
sec.p: Three different types of coffee were selected for the immersion protocol: Turkish coffee, filter coffee, and instant coffee. To ensure standardization of the source, all coffee products were obtained from the same manufacturer (Starbucks, Seattle, WA, USA). According to the manufacturer, the coffees were produced from 100% Arabica beans and were imported by Nestlé Turkey.

After baseline color, microhardness, and surface roughness measurements were recorded, the specimens were divided into four subgroups (n = 10) according to the immersion medium, consisting of Turkish coffee, filter coffee, instant coffee, and distilled water. The solutions were prepared according to the manufacturer’s instructions (Table 2):

sec.p: All immersion media, including distilled water and coffee solutions, were adjusted to 37 °C before contact with the specimens, stored in an incubator (Nüve EN 120, Nüve, Ankara, Türkiye) maintained at this temperature throughout the 30-day experimental period, and renewed every 24 h (Table 2). The pH of the coffee solutions was not standardized or adjusted to a common value; instead, each solution was used with its inherent pH as determined by the coffee type and brewing protocol. All 120 specimens (n = 10 per group) were evaluated for color change, surface roughness, and microhardness at baseline, day 7, and day 30.

sec.title: Color measurement
sec.p: All specimens were air-dried and measured three times on a white background under D65 illumination using a CM-26dG sphere spectrophotometer (Konica Minolta, Tokyo, Japan) operating in the CIE L*a*b* color space over a wavelength range of 360–740 nm. The device employs d:8° sphere geometry with simultaneous SCI/SCE acquisition, and all measurements were taken with the medium aperture (MAV, 8 mm) and the CIE 2° standard observer. Before measurements, the device was calibrated using the manufacturer’s white calibration plate and re-calibrated after every 10 measurements [9, 10]. For each specimen, three consecutive readings were obtained, and the mean L*, a*, and b* values were calculated. Chroma (C*) and hue angle (h°) values were derived from the a* and b* coordinates using standard CIELAB equations (C* = (a*² + b*²)¹ᐟ² and h° = arctangent (b*/a*), with hue angle values adjusted to the appropriate quadrant) [13]. Color difference values (ΔE00) were then calculated using the CIEDE2000 formula with the parametric factors set to kL = kC = kH = 1 [14, 15].
The CIEDE2000 (ΔE00) perceptibility threshold (PT) was set at 0.8 and the acceptability threshold (AT) at 1.8, and the results were interpreted according to these thresholds [16].

sec.title: Surface roughness measurement
sec.p: Surface roughness (Ra) values of all specimens were measured using a confocal microscope (Zeiss Smartproof 5; Carl Zeiss, Germany) with analysis software (ConfoMap ST; Carl Zeiss, Germany). Images were acquired with a 20× objective lens. For each specimen, Ra was measured in three different regions and the measurements were averaged to obtain a single Ra value [17].

sec.title: Microhardness measurement
sec.p: The surface microhardness values of all specimens were measured with a Vickers hardness tester (HMV-2000; Shimadzu, Germany), and values were recorded as Vickers Hardness Number (VHN). A 0.49 N load was applied with a dwell time of 15 s. Three indentations were made on each specimen, centered and spaced 100 μm apart and the mean of these three measurements was calculated [18].

sec.title: CGA and TPC analysis of coffees
sec.p: Chlorogenic acid (CGA) and total phenolic content (TPC) of the three coffee solutions were analyzed simultaneously. Coffee samples were prepared according to the same preparation protocols used for the immersion solutions of the composite specimens. CGA and TPC analyses were performed on separate samples taken from the freshly prepared coffee solutions. All samples were freshly prepared and analyzed immediately after cooling to room temperature [19].

sec.title: Chemicals
sec.p: Gallic acid was purchased from Merck (Istanbul, Türkiye). Folin–Ciocalteu’s phenol reagent and other chemicals were obtained from Sigma-Aldrich (Istanbul, Türkiye). Chlorogenic acid (CGA) standard, chloroform, and calcium carbonate (CaCO₃) were also procured for CGA quantification.

sec.title: Determination of Total Phenolic Content (TPC)
sec.p: The total phenolic content of the coffee samples was determined using the Folin–Ciocalteu method with minor modifications [20]. Briefly, the Folin–Ciocalteu reagent was diluted with distilled water and mixed with appropriately diluted coffee samples or standard solutions of gallic acid (800, 400, 200, 100, 50, 25, 12.5, 6.25, 3.125, 1.5625 µg/mL). Sodium carbonate (Na₂CO₃) solution was then added, and the mixtures were incubated in the dark at room temperature for 2 h. Absorbance was measured at 765 nm using a spectrophotometer (BMG Labtech SPECTROstar Nano, Ortenberg, Germany). All measurements were performed in triplicate, and results were expressed as mg gallic acid equivalents (GAE) per cup of coffee [21].

sec.title: Spectrophotometric determination of chlorogenic acid (CGA)
sec.p: CGA content was analyzed using a modified spectrophotometric method. A 1000 ppm CGA stock solution was prepared by dissolving 5 mg of CGA in 5 mL distilled water, and working standard solutions (10, 20, 30, 40 ppm) were prepared from the stock. Absorbance was recorded from 200 to 400 nm, with λmax observed at ~ 325 nm, to construct a calibration curve.

For sample preparation, 50 mL of each coffee solution was basified with 1.5 g CaCO₃, followed by six sequential chloroform extractions (25 mL each) to remove caffeine and isolate CGA. The aqueous layers (analysis solutions) were appropriately diluted and measured at 325 nm using a UV-VIS spectrophotometer (GBC Cintra 303; GBC Scientific Equipment Pty Ltd, Melbourne, Australia). Measurements were performed in triplicate against a distilled water blank. CGA concentrations were calculated from the calibration curve and expressed as mg per cup [19].

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Statistical analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics version 25 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). Normality was assessed using the Shapiro–Wilk test, and homogeneity of variances using Levene’s test. Given the three-factor design of the study, microhardness (VHN), surface roughness (Ra), and color change (ΔE00) were analyzed using a mixed-design three-way ANOVA, in which Time was treated as a within-subjects factor and Material and Solution as between-subjects factors. Main effects and interaction terms were reported with the corresponding F, p, and partial eta-squared (ηp²) values, and Bonferroni-adjusted post hoc tests were applied for multiple comparisons (α = 0.05). In addition, Pearson correlation analysis was conducted on the 30-day data to evaluate the relationships among ΔE00, Ra, VHN, and the coffee composition parameters (TPC and CGA). For descriptive purposes, 95% confidence intervals were also provided in the results tables.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Pearson correlation analysis based on the 30-day measurements revealed a moderate, negative correlation between surface roughness and microhardness (Ra–VHN; r = − 0.43, p < 0.001), indicating that higher roughness was associated with lower hardness. The correlation between Ra and color change (ΔE00) was weak but statistically significant (r = − 0.19, p = 0.040), whereas the relationship between VHN and ΔE00 was weak and not statistically significant (p > 0.05).

sec.title: Color Change (ΔE00)
sec.p: In relation to the data presented in Table 3, within-subjects analysis showed a significant main effect of time on ΔE00 (Pillai’s trace = 0.234, F(1,108) = 33.067, p < 0.001, partial η² = 0.234), indicating that ΔE00 values increased over time. The Time × Material interaction was not significant (p = 0.83), whereas the Time × Solution interaction was significant (Pillai’s trace = 0.103, F(3,108) = 4.127, p = 0.008, partial η² = 0.10), demonstrating that the rate of discoloration differed mainly among solutions rather than among materials. Pairwise comparisons showed that the change in ΔE00 from day 7 to day 30 was not significant in distilled water and filter coffee (p > 0.05), whereas Turkish coffee and instant coffee exhibited significantly higher ΔE00 values at day 30 than at day 7 (both p < 0.001). At day 30, instant coffee caused the most pronounced discoloration, with ΔE₀₀ values significantly higher than those of all other solutions (p < 0.001; Table 3). Turkish coffee and filter coffee exhibited similar levels of discoloration (p > 0.05). All coffee solutions caused greater color change than distilled water (instant coffee > Turkish coffee ≈ filter coffee > distilled water; p < 0.001). Although no significant difference in discoloration was found between FU and ESQ (p > 0.05), GA showed significantly lower discoloration than both materials (FU ≈ ESQ > GA; p < 0.001, Table 3).

sec.title: Surface roughness
sec.p: Surface roughness increased significantly over time in all materials (Pillai’s trace = 0.634, F(2,107) = 92.718, p < 0.001, partial η² = 0.634) (Table 4). At the between-subjects level, the main effect of material [F(2,108) = 49.411, p < 0.001, partial η² = 0.48], the main effect of solution [F(3,108) = 3.893, p = 0.011, partial η² = 0.10], and the Material × Solution interaction [F(6,108) = 3.716, p = 0.002, partial η² = 0.17] were all statistically significant. The time-dependent increase in roughness varied according to the type of solution. After 30 days, filter coffee produced the greatest increase in roughness, whereas instant coffee caused the smallest increase; however, pairwise comparisons among the coffee groups were not statistically significant (p > 0.05). Among the resin composites, GA, which already exhibited relatively high baseline roughness, reached the highest roughness values at day 30 (Table 4; Figs. 1, 2 and 3). At day 30, the roughness ranking among the composites was GA > ESQ > FU, and all pairwise comparisons were statistically significant (GA–ESQ and GA–FU: p < 0.001; ESQ–FU: p = 0.004).

sec.title: Microhardness
sec.p: Microhardness decreased significantly over time across all materials, and a strong main effect of time was detected (Pillai’s trace = 0.683; F(2,107) = 115.287; p < 0.001; partial η² = 0.683). At day 30, the mean hardness losses by solution were approximately 14.1% in distilled water, 15.2% in filter coffee, 7.9% in Turkish coffee, and 15.0% in instant coffee (Table 5). For FU, significant reductions were found in distilled water and filter coffee at all time points (p = 0.021 and p = 0.046), only at 30 days in instant coffee (p < 0.001), and no significant changes were detected in Turkish coffee (p > 0.05; Table 5). For ESQ, significant reductions were observed at 7 and 30 days in distilled water and Turkish coffee (p = 0.003 and p = 0.001, respectively), and at all time points in filter and instant coffee (p < 0.05). For GA, significant decreases were found at 7 and 30 days in distilled water and filter coffee, at both time points in Turkish coffee, and at all time points in instant coffee (p < 0.05; Table 5). Consistent with these patterns, the Time × Solution interaction was significant (Pillai’s trace = 0.212; F(6, 216) = 4.274; p < 0.001; partial η² = 0.11), whereas the Time × Material interaction was not (p = 0.29). This indicates that, although absolute hardness levels differed among composites, the time-dependent pattern of hardness loss was broadly similar across materials, with the main divergence occurring at the solution level. The three-way Time × Material × Solution interaction was also significant (p = 0.024; partial η² = 0.10), indicating that specific material–solution combinations responded differently over time. At the between-subjects level, the main effect of Material was very strong [F(2,108) = 289.258, p < 0.001, partial η² = 0.843], showing that the hardness level was largely dependent on material composition. In our study, considering all time points, FU showed the highest microhardness, followed by ESQ and GA, with all pairwise differences being significant (ESQ–GA: p = 0.002; FU–ESQ and FU–GA: p < 0.001).

sec.title: Phenolic content and chlorogenic acid levels of coffee preparations
sec.p: The brewing ratios, total phenolic content (TPC), and chlorogenic acid (CGA) levels of the different coffee preparations are presented in Table 6. The total phenolic contents were calculated using the equation (y = 0.0027x + 0.1187, R² = 0.9955) derived from the calibration curve of gallic acid. Using the CGA calibration curve, the CGA content was quantified with the equation (y = 0.0514x- 0.0692, R² = 0.9903). Instant coffee had the highest TPC (1353.94 ± 53.36 mg GAE/cup) and CGA (433.98 ± 0.19 mg/cup) values. Turkish coffee had the lowest TPC (157.18 ± 48.12 mg GAE/cup), whereas filter coffee exhibited the lowest CGA content (168.50 ± 0.21 mg/cup; Table 6).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Exposure of resin composite materials to commonly consumed staining agents such as coffee effects not only their color stability but also surface properties, including roughness and microhardness, thereby influencing their long-term esthetic and functional performance [3]. Thus, in-vitro immersion studies with coffee solutions are particularly relevant for predicting restorative material durability. However, there is limited evidence comparing the effects of different coffee brewing methods, and no consensus exists regarding which type causes the most surface degradation—an important gap for clinical decision-making and patient counseling. In this study, 30-day exposure of three universal resin composites to different coffee types significantly effected surface roughness, microhardness, and color stability. Both immersion time and coffee type influenced all parameters; thus, the first null hypothesis was rejected (p < 0.05). In addition, CGA and TPC levels showed significant differences among the coffee types, and therefore the second null hypothesis of the study was also rejected.

In the present study, all composites exhibited an increase in surface roughness over time, although the magnitude of this change depended on the type of immersion solution. The higher surface roughness values observed at day 30 in the filter coffee group compared with the distilled water group suggest that this solution may exert an additional mechanical or semi-mechanical abrasive effect on the surface. This is consistent with previous reports indicating that acidic and pigmented beverages can soften the resin matrix, leading to filler particle loss and surface degradation [22, 23]. Nevertheless, none of the materials exceeded the critical 0.2 μm threshold for plaque accumulation [9], likely due to their nanostructure and careful polishing. Regarding composites, GA exhibited the highest roughness, ESQ an intermediate level, and FU the lowest—consistent with evidence that smaller filler particles reduce roughness [24]. SEM (Scanning Electron Microscope) analyses confirmed that GA contains larger, irregular fillers (300 nm barium glass + 16 nm fumed silica, HPC (High Performance Pulverized CERASMART), which created more surface irregularities after polishing [25, 26]. ESQ’s spherical fillers promoted smoother surfaces [27, 28], while FU’s nanoclusters (20 nm silica + 4–11 nm zirconia) and compact matrix accounted for its lowest values [29]. The greater solubility of GA’s barium fillers may also have contributed to matrix degradation. While our findings align with most studies [25, 29, 30], Gurgan et al. (2022) reported FU as rougher than suprananohybrid composites, attributing this to filler type and matrix composition [24–26].

Surface hardness is essential for maintaining restoration form stability and wear resistance [31, 32]. In our study, FU exhibited the highest microhardness, followed by ESQ and GA. These differences may result from variations in cross-linking density, resin matrix type, and filler characteristics [33]. Although higher filler loading is generally associated with greater hardness [33], both GA (82 wt %) and ESQ (82 wt %) showed lower hardness values than FU (76.5 wt %), in line with previous reports [33, 34]. FU’s zirconia/silica clusters and ytterbium trifluoride fillers likely contribute to its superior hardness [34]. The literature indicates that materials with a higher degree of cross-linking and greater filler content generally exhibit superior surface hardness [35]. FU’s organic matrix is composed of AUDMA (Aromatic Urethane Dimethacrylate), AFM (Addition–Fragmentation Monomer), diurethane dimethacrylate, and 1,12-dodecane dimethacrylate. AUDMA, owing to its high molecular weight, reduces polymerization shrinkage, whereas AFM operates through a controlled fragmentation–recombination mechanism to relieve stress during polymerization. Together, these monomers promote a high degree of cross-linking, thereby enhancing mechanical strength and marginal integrity [36, 37]. With respect to immersion media, filter and instant coffee produced the greatest microhardness losses after 30 days, distilled water caused moderate reductions, whereas Turkish coffee resulted in the smallest change, with hardness loss even slightly lower than that observed in distilled water. Although coffee components are known to chemically weaken the polymer matrix [31], the microhardness losses observed in the coffee groups were close to, or in the case of Turkish coffee even lower than, those in the distilled water group, suggesting that the additional effect of coffee on microhardness may be limited and that these findings should be interpreted with caution from a clinical perspective.

Coffee is considered one of the most potent staining agents for resin composites [38]. In this study, all solutions produced a numerical increase in ΔE₀₀ values by day 30; however, this increase was statistically significant only in the Turkish coffee and instant coffee groups, and not in the filter coffee or distilled water groups. Resin composite specimens stored in distilled water exceeded the perceptibility threshold (ΔE₀₀ = 0.8) at days 7 and 30, but their ΔE₀₀ values generally remained below the acceptability threshold of 1.8. In contrast, in the filter, Turkish, and instant coffee groups, ΔE₀₀ values at both time points exceeded the acceptability threshold, indicating clinically noticeable discoloration [16, 39, 40]. The non-significant Time × Material interaction, together with the significant Time × Solution interaction, indicates that the progression of discoloration over time was governed mainly by the type of coffee solution rather than by the composite material itself.

Although nanohybrid composites are designed to provide smoother surfaces due to their multi-sized filler particles [4] smaller filler size does not necessarily correlate with less discoloration, as the monomer composition also plays a role [4, 5]. In this context, ESQ which contains a more hydrophilic Bis-GMA (bisphenol A-glycidyl methacrylate)/TEGDMA (triethylene glycol dimethacrylate)-based resin matrix, may be more prone to water sorption and solubility, thereby facilitating pigment diffusion and discoloration compared with the Bis-GMA–free, UDMA/Bis-MPEPP-based matrix of GA. This interpretation is in line with reports that hydrophilic monomers, particularly TEGDMA, are associated with higher water sorption and greater color change [41–43].

These considerations are also consistent with previous reports indicating that FU shows greater coffee-induced staining than GA [44, 45]. The functional monomers AUDMA and AFM in FU contribute to reducing polymerization shrinkage, but their lower hydrophobicity compared to Bis-GMA may increase pigment absorption and accelerate discoloration [45]. In contrast, GA is formulated without Bis-GMA, incorporating UDMA (Urethane Dimethacrylate) and Bis-MPEPP (2,2-bis (4-methacryloxy polyethoxyphenyl) propane) monomers and reinforced with FSC (Full-coverage Silane Coating) -treated barium glass and fumed silica fillers. These structural features may help explain its superior color stability [44, 46].

Coffee’s chemical composition plays a key role in composite discoloration and degradation [2, 3]. Phenolic compounds, particularly CGA and tannins, contribute to pigment formation, with TPC levels serving as an indicator of staining potential [2, 3]. Our results support this, as instant coffee—with the highest TPC and CGA—caused the most discoloration, followed by Turkish coffee. Our TPC and CGA analyses confirmed that instant coffee contained the highest levels of phenolic compounds, which is in line with previous reports [11, 12]. This chemical profile is consistent with the markedly higher ΔE₀₀ values observed in the instant coffee group. Coffee is one of the most commonly used staining agents in laboratory studies to simulate daily consumption habits [38]. In resin-based composites, discoloration occurs through adsorption and absorption of yellow pigments into the organic matrix [47]. According to the literature, a cup of coffee is typically consumed within 15 min, with an average daily intake of approximately 3.2 cups [48]. Based on this, 72 h of simulated immersion corresponds to about 3 months of consumption, whereas the 720 h applied in the present study represents approximately 30 months of coffee intake. Different brewing methods of the same coffee type can lead to significant variations in TPC levels. The high TPC content of instant coffees may be attributed to the industrial drying process, in which water evaporation concentrates phenolic compounds. It has been reported that instant coffee exhibits the highest TPC values, and other studies have similarly demonstrated higher TPC levels in instant products compared to brewed ground coffee [30, 49, 50].

Among the tested coffees, the most pronounced increase in surface roughness was observed in filter coffee, whereas the lowest effect was found in instant coffee. This may be related to the fact that filter coffee brews prepared from ground coffee have a different chemical and physicochemical profile than instant coffee. While the staining and acidic properties of coffee can induce both physical and chemical changes in composites, it has been reported that mildly acidic pH may also indirectly enhance discoloration by promoting the proliferation of acidophilic bacteria [11]. In addition, it has been shown that the brewing parameters used with ground coffee (grinding degree, water/coffee ratio, time, filter type, and temperature) significantly effect the levels of dissolved and undissolved solids, melanoidins, and lipid fractions, whereas instant coffee, as a result of industrial extraction and drying, is a more homogeneous product containing fewer particles [11, 12]. When the resin matrix is softened by organic acids and phenolic compounds, as suggested by studies showing that polyphenol content and antioxidant activity vary with coffee type and preparation method [49, 51], repeated exposure to particle- and colloid-rich filter coffee may increase selective matrix loss and filler exposure, thereby elevating surface roughness [30]. In contrast, clearer and more homogeneous instant coffee solutions may facilitate the diffusion of chromogens into the resin matrix and promote discoloration without inducing a comparable level of abrasive effect [30, 48].

In the present study, surface roughness and microhardness showed a moderate, inverse correlation at day 30, indicating that specimens with more pronounced surface degradation tended to exhibit lower hardness values. This pattern is consistent with previous reports suggesting that a decrease in microhardness is indicative of superficial degradation and is often accompanied by increased roughness in resin composites [51, 52]. The correlation between surface roughness and color change was weak and not clinically relevant, indicating that variations in ΔE₀₀ were largely independent of Ra in this study. This suggests that, under the present conditions, discoloration was influenced more by material composition and the staining solution than by surface roughness [53]. No significant correlation was found between microhardness and color change, suggesting that staining susceptibility is largely independent of hardness. Rather, color stability appears to be governed mainly by resin matrix composition, water sorption, and interactions with staining solutions [54, 55].

This study has several limitations. Because it was conducted under in-vitro conditions, dynamic intraoral factors such as salivary flow, pellicle formation, pH and temperature fluctuations, and individual diet/oral hygiene habits could not be fully reproduced. The fact that the staining protocol did not include toothbrushing with toothpaste or mechanical/thermal aging procedures (e.g., brushing simulation, thermocycling) means that the observed discoloration and surface changes may only partially reflect clinical conditions. The limited number of coffee types/brands tested and the use of a 30-day immersion protocol, which only partially represents long-term intraoral exposure, also restrict the generalizability of the findings. Another limitation is that the pH values of the solutions were not measured, making it difficult to assess the specific contribution of coffee acidity independently from phenolic compounds and CGA. Coffee chemistry parameters (TPC and CGA) were analyzed only at the solution level (a single value per beverage type), whereas ΔE₀₀, Ra, and VHN were measured at the specimen level (n = 10). Since TPC and CGA did not vary within groups, formal regression or correlation analyses with the composite outcomes were not performed, and the relationships were instead interpreted descriptively. Future studies should investigate different coffee additives, coffee types and brands, and enamel substrates, in designs that also account for pH and other beverage components, to clarify more precisely the specific role of CGA in discoloration.

Despite these limitations, this study determined the CGA and TPC contents of three different coffee types and related these findings to changes in the discoloration, roughness, and microhardness of composite resins. The use of coffee solutions prepared according to a standardized protocol provides additional methodological strength, and the study offers a comprehensive and original contribution to the coffee-related staining literature by jointly considering both material properties and coffee composition.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: The findings of this study indicate that different coffee types significantly affect the color stability, surface roughness, and microhardness of resin composite with instant coffee—having the highest TPC and CGA levels—causing the most pronounced discoloration. Among the materials evaluated, the Bis-GMA–free, UDMA/Bis-MPEPP–based nanohybrid composite (GA) showed relatively greater resistance to coffee-induced surface changes, suggesting that composites with more hydrophobic resin matrices and optimized filler technology may be preferable for patients with high coffee consumption. Overall, the results highlight that dietary habits, particularly frequent coffee intake, play a clinically important role in the long-term esthetic and functional performance of resin-based restorations, underscoring the need to address coffee consumption during patient counselling and to consider these factors in material selection.
